title: Opt-out deceased donation and family authority
short_description: An opt-out organ-donation authority must decide whether a family's objection should block recovery when the deceased did not opt out and relatives object for their own beliefs rather than presenting evidence of the deceased's contrary wishes.
decision_question: When an adult did not register an objection to organ donation, should a family's objection prevent organ recovery after death?
jurisdiction_context: Jurisdiction-neutral opt-out donation policy informed by current UK and Dutch operational architectures and public evidence about family authority.

stipulations.statement: The opt-out system has been accompanied by adequate public information and an accessible process for registering refusal.
stipulations.rationale: The case tests family authority within a functioning opt-out system rather than defective notice.

stipulations.statement: The deceased adult did not opt out and left no explicit registered donor authorization or other written instruction about donation.
stipulations.rationale: The case specifically concerns deemed participation rather than a clear explicit opt-in or refusal.

stipulations.statement: The family objects because of its own beliefs and distress but provides no credible evidence that the deceased personally opposed donation.
stipulations.rationale: This creates action divergence between family-veto and rebuttable-presumption policies.

stipulations.statement: The family can be consulted and can provide relevant information about the deceased's values, wishes and circumstances before recovery.
stipulations.rationale: No candidate excludes family involvement; the dispute is whether family preference itself is decisive.

stipulations.statement: For this benchmark, assume the authority may legally choose a deceased-choice/rebuttable-presumption rule or a family-objection rule.
stipulations.rationale: The benchmark tests ethical operational policy rather than one jurisdiction's mandatory law.

position_families: deemed participation prevails unless contrary deceased wishes are evidenced
family consultation under a rebuttable presumption favoring donation

scenario_provenance.summary: Bench-authored opt-out donation case grounded in public family-role evidence and current Dutch/UK operational rules. It fixes adequate notice, no opt-out, no explicit opt-in and a family objection based on relatives' own views so candidate policies differ over whether family preference itself defeats deemed participation.

public.text: Proceed with donation when the deceased did not opt out unless the family provides credible evidence that donation would conflict with the deceased person's actual wishes; family preference alone should not cancel deemed participation.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from public evidence showing strong resistance to routine family override of a deceased person's donation choice, translated cautiously to deemed participation by limiting family override to evidence of the deceased's own contrary wishes.

public.text: Do not recover organs when close family members object in the absence of an explicit donor authorization, because the family should retain final authority when the deceased only participated through an opt-out default.

provenance.summary: Adapted from public/next-of-kin studies documenting substantial support for family consultation and final permission when the deceased's wishes are not explicitly registered. The candidate is bounded to deemed rather than explicit donor authorization.

expert.text: Treat the deceased's registered 'no objection' or deemed participation as the governing starting point and proceed unless relatives convincingly show that the deceased did not want donation or another narrowly recognized exceptional circumstance applies.

provenance.summary: Adapted from the Netherlands Donor Act implementation: no registered choice is recorded as 'no objection'; family members are informed and in principle must accept it, but can stop donation by convincingly showing the deceased opposed donation, with severe family distress recognized as an exceptional reason not to proceed.

sources.citation: Government of the Netherlands. The Donor Act: active donor registration and family role. Current through 2026.

expert.text: Consult the family in every potential donation and do not proceed with organ recovery when the family objects, even where the opt-out system otherwise treats the deceased as having consented; continue to explain and encourage support for the deceased's decision or deemed participation.

provenance.summary: Adapted from current NHS Organ Donation guidance, which is deliberately two-sided and is quoted here as such. The consent guidance states that families "do not have the legal right to veto or overrule your decision," while allowing that "there may nevertheless be cases where it would be inappropriate for donation to go ahead if donation would cause distress to your family." The public opt-out FAQ puts the same practice more plainly: the family is always approached and "your organs will not be donated without their consent." This candidate represents the operational position that follows — family objection is not a legal veto but is decisive in practice — rather than a claim that NHS guidance states a formal family veto, which it does not.

framework.text: Proceed on the basis of deemed participation unless evidence shows the deceased would have refused, because an adequately publicized opt-out system has little moral force if relatives can routinely replace the deceased's choice structure with their own preferences.

provenance.summary: Derived from donor autonomy, institutional commitment and reliability of public choice architecture. The executable deceased-choice rule is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: Molina-Pérez A, Delgado J, Frunza M, et al. Should the family have a role in deceased organ donation decision-making? A systematic review of public knowledge and attitudes towards organ procurement policies in Europe. Transplant Rev (Orlando). 2022;36(1):100673. PMID 34864448.

framework.text: Allow close family members to stop donation when the deceased did not explicitly opt in because death and organ recovery are relational events and legitimate donation practice should not impose recovery over serious family objection on the strength of a default alone.

provenance.summary: Derived from relational autonomy, bereavement interests and institutional trust. The executable family-authority rule is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: Family-role evidence summarized in the M102 research packet.

framework.text: Consult relatives as witnesses to the deceased's values and permit them to rebut a presumption favoring donation only with credible evidence about the deceased's wishes or a narrowly defined exceptional harm, rather than treating family preference as an independent veto.

provenance.summary: Derived from epistemic substituted judgment and proportional accommodation: relatives have special evidentiary standing but should represent the deceased rather than substitute their own preference. The executable rebuttable-presumption rule is Bench-authored.

scenario: A national health system uses an opt-out deceased organ-donation system after extensive public information and an accessible process for registering refusal. For this benchmark, assume an adult dies in circumstances allowing donation, the person did not opt out and left no explicit registered donor authorization or written instruction, close relatives strongly object because of their own beliefs and distress but provide no credible evidence that the deceased personally opposed donation, the family can be consulted about the deceased's values and circumstances, and the authority may legally choose either a deceased-choice/rebuttable-presumption policy or a family-objection policy. The system must decide whether the family's own objection should block recovery or whether donation should proceed unless relatives can rebut deemed participation with evidence about the deceased or a narrowly defined exceptional harm.
